strengths: This is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. DF3DV-1K addresses a clear computer-vision need: existing distractor-free novel-view-synthesis datasets contain only 5–12 public scenes, whereas the proposed dataset contains 1,048 scenes and 89,924 images, including paired clean and cluttered captures.

The collection is unusually broad for this task: 726 indoor and 322 outdoor scenes, 128 distractor types, 161 themes, 12 consumer cameras, multiple resolutions, and nine months of acquisition. DF3DV-41 additionally targets 17 deliberately challenging scenarios such as semantically similar, reflective, fluid, and semi-transparent distractors.

The acquisition and curation pipeline is sensible. Joint COLMAP registration places clean and cluttered observations in a common coordinate system; manual quality screening and instant-ngp reconstruction provide useful quality-control stages.

Benchmarking nine specialized methods plus 3DGS over all 1,048 scenes is a substantial computational contribution. Evaluations on RobustNeRF, On-the-go, DF3DV-1K, and DF3DV-41 expose meaningful changes in method ranking and challenging conditions that small existing benchmarks do not reveal.

The secondary DI2FIX study demonstrates that the collection can support learned, cross-scene models rather than only evaluation. It includes held-out DF3DV-41 and external On-the-go testing, data-scale and filtering-threshold ablations, and leave-one-method-out evaluation. The reported mean gain of 0.96 dB PSNR and reduction of 0.057 LPIPS are practically meaningful.

The paper is generally clear, well illustrated, appropriately situated relative to distractor-free, in-the-wild, and dynamic radiance-field work, and candidly notes several limitations of DI2FIX and the captures.
weaknesses: The core dataset contribution is not yet sufficiently reproducible from the supplied manuscript. There is no dataset or code URL, explicit release commitment or schedule, license, file-format description, dataset card, benchmark API, or preservation plan. Since the paper motivates itself partly through the absence of a public large-scale dataset, availability is central rather than incidental.

Essential benchmark details are deferred to an unavailable supplement (e.g., Sec. S.2 and Tables S.1–S.5). The main paper does not specify train/test construction, image resizing, method-specific hyperparameters, stopping rules, random seeds, failure handling, or whether results are aggregated per image or per scene. These choices could materially affect rankings across 10 heterogeneous methods.

The paper reports only aggregate point estimates, without uncertainty, repeated-run variation, scene-level distributions for method comparisons, or statistical tests. DF3DV-41 scenario groups may contain very few scenes, but their group sizes are not reported, weakening conclusions about which distractor categories are intrinsically hardest.

The claim that DF3DV-1K is more difficult specifically because of distractors is not cleanly established. Lower 3DGS scores can also result from harder geometry, exposure changes, different camera devices, view coverage, pose error, or temporal illumination changes between clean and cluttered captures. A controlled comparison using clean-only versus cluttered training on the same scenes would better isolate distractor difficulty.

Dataset documentation is incomplete. The manuscript gives counts for manually assigned themes and distractor types but does not define the taxonomy, report annotation agreement, explain multi-label treatment, quantify capture-pair temporal gaps, or provide pose/reconstruction quality statistics and rejection rates.

For outdoor data containing passers-by, vehicles, and private environments, the manuscript does not discuss consent, privacy filtering for faces or license plates, geographic bias, ownership, or permitted redistribution. These are important release considerations for a large real-world dataset.

DI2FIX is a useful demonstration but has limited algorithmic novelty, being primarily DIFIX fine-tuning with a changed reference input. Its inference protocol is underspecified, and a framewise 2D enhancer may hallucinate content or introduce cross-view inconsistency; the evaluation contains neither temporal/multiview consistency measurements nor a human perceptual study.

The data-scale experiment does not isolate scale from diversity: independently random subsets of 250, 500, and 750 scenes naturally change both. Multiple subset draws or diversity-matched controls are needed to substantiate the claim that both factors drive the improvement. Overall, the dataset's scale and likely impact support a slight preference for acceptance, but release, protocol, and governance details should be resolved.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than the default Algorithms/General type. Under that framing, the scale is potentially significant: DF3DV-1K contains 1,048 paired clean/cluttered scenes, 89,924 images, 726 indoor and 322 outdoor scenes, 128 reported distractor types, and data from 12 consumer devices collected over nine months.

Benchmarking ten methods over all 1,048 scenes represents substantial computational and engineering effort. The results expose meaningful differences among recent distractor-removal methods and identify difficult conditions such as semantically similar distractors, fluids, and nighttime scenes.

The collection pipeline is reasonably motivated and includes manual quality review, joint COLMAP reconstruction, image undistortion, instant-ngp verification, and metadata annotation. The inclusion of both clean and cluttered views enables quantitative evaluation that many related datasets cannot support.

DF3DV-41 is a useful attempt to complement aggregate benchmarking with controlled, scenario-wise analysis. The paper is generally readable and provides clear dataset statistics, comparisons with prior datasets, and qualitative examples.

DI2FIX provides an illustrative downstream use of the dataset. Its held-out evaluation on DF3DV-41 and On-the-go reports an average improvement from 20.82 to 21.78 dB PSNR and from 0.211 to 0.154 LPIPS, while the data-scale ablation shows a consistent trend.
weaknesses: The benchmark protocol is not specified with enough precision in the supplied manuscript to establish reproducibility or fairness. Essential details—including exact image splits, per-method configurations and tuning, initialization and failure handling, resolution and preprocessing, metric aggregation, and compute allocation—are deferred to supplementary sections that are not present in the supplied PDF.

The central claim that DF3DV-1K is more difficult than earlier datasets is supported mainly by lower absolute PSNR/SSIM and higher LPIPS across different scenes. These values are confounded by scene geometry, view extrapolation, illumination, camera quality, pose error, and image resolution, so they do not isolate distractor difficulty. A controlled comparison using matched corruption levels or performance relative to clean-trained upper bounds is needed.

Camera poses are jointly estimated from clean and cluttered images. Because the clean images also serve as evaluation targets, this introduces test-set information into preprocessing and does not reflect the claimed setting of reconstruction from cluttered inputs alone. The paper should quantify the effect of clean-image-assisted pose estimation and provide a clutter-only pose protocol.

The dataset taxonomy and curation lack validation. The manuscript reports 128 distractor types and 161 themes but does not provide the full ontology, labeling rules, frequency distribution in the main paper, multi-label policy, or inter-annotator agreement. The construction and selection criteria for the 41-scene challenge subset are also insufficiently documented, leaving room for selection bias.

Results are reported almost exclusively as global means or per-image distributions, without scene-balanced statistics, variance, confidence intervals, significance testing, or analysis of failures and excluded scenes. Unequal numbers of images per scene can cause large scenes to dominate the reported ranking.

The argument that rankings roughly following publication chronology demonstrates benchmark reliability is not scientifically convincing; chronology is neither a ground-truth ordering nor evidence of validity. Several ranking differences are also small enough that uncertainty estimates could change the conclusions.

DI2FIX is a 2D diffusion enhancer rather than a demonstrated improvement to 3D reconstruction. Evaluation uses only frame-wise full-reference image metrics, with no multi-view consistency, geometric accuracy, hallucination analysis, or user study. Consequently, the claim that it improves radiance-field rendering is stronger than the evidence supports, especially given the acknowledged confirmation-bias failure mode.

The data-scale ablation changes both the number and diversity of scenes, so it cannot support the stated conclusion that both factors are responsible. DI2FIX results are additionally pooled across datasets and base methods, obscuring where gains or regressions occur; the detailed per-method evidence is again deferred to unavailable supplementary material.

For a dataset contribution, release and governance details are critical but missing: there is no concrete availability statement, license, hosting plan, dataset card, consent/privacy treatment for public scenes or identifiable people, or documentation of geographic and demographic biases. These omissions materially weaken reproducibility and responsible reuse.

Overall, the collection could become a valuable community resource, but the current evidence and documentation do not yet make the benchmark sufficiently auditable. The scale and effort keep the work near the acceptance boundary, while protocol ambiguity, confounded difficulty claims, missing statistical analysis, and absent release/governance details favor a borderline reject.

strengths: This is a strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution addressing a clear gap: existing public distractor-free novel-view-synthesis datasets contain only 5–12 scenes, whereas DF3DV-1K provides 1,048 paired clean/cluttered scenes and 89,924 images.

The collection is unusually broad and practically relevant, covering 726 indoor and 322 outdoor scenes, 161 themes, 128 distractor types, 12 consumer capture devices, and nine months of acquisition. The use of casual consumer-camera capture improves relevance to real deployment conditions.

The dataset construction is thoughtful: clean and cluttered views share a coordinate system; images undergo manual quality review, COLMAP processing, and instant-ngp reconstruction verification; and DF3DV-41 deliberately targets 17 difficult conditions such as fluid, semantically similar, reflective, and semi-transparent distractors.

The benchmark is extensive and valuable, evaluating nine recent distractor-removal approaches plus vanilla 3DGS across all 1,048 scenes. Its approximately 2.03 GPU-years of evaluation and inclusion of established RobustNeRF and On-the-go benchmarks make the resulting comparison a substantial community resource.

The experiments produce actionable findings rather than only introducing data: AsymGS and RobustSplat emerge as the strongest overall methods, while scenario-level analysis identifies semantically similar and fluid distractors and nighttime scenes as important unresolved cases.

DI2FIX is a useful feasibility demonstration of the dataset's value for learning generalizable models. It improves the averaged held-out result by 0.96 dB PSNR and 0.057 LPIPS, includes data-scale and pair-selection ablations, and is evaluated on both DF3DV-41 and the external On-the-go dataset.

The paper is clearly motivated, well organized, visually polished, and unusually careful not to overstate shortcomings of prior datasets. It also acknowledges failure under severe corruption and possible confirmation bias.
weaknesses: For a dataset paper, release and reproducibility information is insufficiently explicit in the supplied manuscript: there is no clear release URL, license, data-access commitment, code/configuration plan, or durable benchmark protocol. Essential implementation details are deferred to a supplementary Sec. S.2 that is not present in the supplied PDF.

The headline dataset-difficulty comparison is not fully controlled. Lower PSNR/SSIM or higher LPIPS across different datasets can reflect scene content, viewpoint distribution, image allocation, resolution, and test-set construction rather than distractor difficulty alone. The claim that rankings roughly following publication time supports benchmark reliability is also not a convincing validation criterion.

DF3DV-41 contains only 41 scenes distributed across 17 scenarios. The paper reports scenario-wise conclusions without uncertainty estimates, repeated captures, confidence intervals, or significance tests; consequently, claims about the hardest distractor categories may be sensitive to a few scenes. It is also unclear whether aggregate metrics are averaged per image or per scene.

Annotation and curation quality control needs more documentation. Although two experts inspect each scene, the manuscript does not report an ontology-development procedure, annotation agreement, adjudication, category frequencies in the main paper, or quantitative checks that clean sets are truly distractor-free.

Camera poses are jointly estimated from clean and cluttered images. This provides pose estimation with information from the clean evaluation collection that would be unavailable in a typical deployment using only cluttered inputs. The benchmark should either justify this oracle-pose setting more explicitly or quantify performance with clutter-only pose estimation.

DI2FIX is a 2D diffusion enhancer, but evaluation is limited mainly to image fidelity metrics. There is no temporal/multiview consistency or geometry assessment, and the method can plausibly hallucinate inconsistent content across novel views. Table 4 also aggregates results across datasets and base methods, obscuring variation in gains in the main paper.

The absence of a substantive privacy, consent, and licensing discussion is notable for 89,924 manually captured indoor and outdoor images, which may contain people, faces, license plates, private spaces, or copyrighted objects. A concrete filtering and redaction policy should accompany release.

Reproducing the full benchmark requires exceptional computation, so providing cached outputs, standardized subsets, and resource-normalized evaluation tracks would materially improve accessibility. These concerns warrant revision but do not outweigh the dataset's scale, relevance, and strong empirical value.
